w: What's tested The cervix: HPV causes the precancers and the cancer, which start where the two linings meet (the transformation zone) Vaginitis: Candida, Trichomonas, and atrophic vaginitis in older women Lichen sclerosus: the itchy, non-infectious skin disease of the vulva that the lecture said can turn into cancer Condyloma acuminatum: benign genital warts from HPV 6 and 11 Age: sarcoma botryoides in girls under 5; squamous cancers in women of reproductive age; lichen sclerosus cancers in older women The breast: ductal versus lobular cancer, Paget disease of the nipple, and the receptors that guide treatment Dr. Dal Zotto, a pathologist, covered the female genital tract from top to bottom, then the breast. These notes follow the recording and the slides. How it forms Two tubes, the paramesonephric ducts, fuse to make the uterus, the upper part of the vagina and the fallopian tubes. The lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus. The uterus sits between the bladder in front and the rectum behind. The uterus The uterus is small, up to 10 centimeters, with the cervix at the bottom and the body above. Its wall is thick smooth muscle, the myometrium, lined inside by a thin glandular lining, the endometrium. The cervix The canal of the cervix is lined by mucus-making glandular cells; the outer part, seen through the vagina, by squamous cells. Where they meet, the transformation zone, the two linings push against each other, the area stays inflamed, and HPV gets in easily. That's where cervical cancer starts; HPV causes more than 90 percent of cervical cancers. It's the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide, less common in the United States because of Pap screening. The HPV vaccine lowers the risk, but it will take decades to see the full effect. Precancer of the cervix The precancers are squamous intraepithelial lesions (also called CIN: low grade is CIN1, high grade CIN2 and CIN3). Low-grade ones can go away; high-grade ones are more likely to become cancer. About 90 percent are from HPV. HPV leaves a mark on cells, the koilocyte: a big nucleus with a clear halo around it. High-grade cells have big, uneven nuclei and little cytoplasm. Once the abnormal cells break through into the tissue under the lining, it's squamous cell carcinoma. Screening is now based on each woman's risk. The body of the uterus The muscle squeezes to stop bleeding each month and to push the baby out. The lining has straight glands in the first half of the cycle (estrogen) and coiled glands after ovulation (progesterone). Chronic endometritis, with plasma cells in the lining, is a common, easily treated cause of infertility: antibiotics fix it. Polyps can hide cancer in older women. Endometrial cancer comes in two types: one driven by extra estrogen (obesity, estrogen without progesterone), less aggressive, in younger women; and an aggressive one in older women, 70 to 80 on the slide (serous and clear cell carcinoma), often spread by the time it's found. Leiomyomas, or fibroids, are very common benign, well-defined muscle lumps that cause heavy bleeding, with no dividing, odd-looking or dead cells; leiomyosarcoma is the rare, aggressive cancer that grows into the tissue around it, with many dividing and odd-looking cells and dead areas, and spreads to the lung. The ovary Most ovarian tumors come from the surface lining (95 percent of ovarian cancers). Ovarian cancer is deadly: aggressive, treated with surgery and a lot of chemotherapy. The vagina Vaginitis is the most common problem. Candida (yeast) shows little sticks under the microscope; Trichomonas, a sexually transmitted parasite, looks like a cell with arms. Older women get atrophic vaginitis, which isn't an infection. Squamous cancers hit women of reproductive age (the slide also lists clear cell adenocarcinoma); sarcoma botryoides, a primitive muscle tumor, hits girls under 5 and does well if treated in time. The vulva Lichen simplex chronicus is skin thickened and leathery from scratching. Lichen sclerosus makes the skin thin, smooth and white like parchment paper; it itches, and it's the one the lecture said can lead to cancer, in older women, without HPV (her slide lists lichen planus too). Lichen planus affects the vulva and the mouth, with a white, lacy pattern: if a patient has both, think lichen planus. The biopsy goes to the lab fresh, and steroids treat it. Genital warts (condyloma acuminatum) come from HPV 6 and 11 and are benign. Vulvar cancer comes either from HPV (type 16 in most) or, in older women, from long-standing inflammation, mostly lichen sclerosus. The breast The breast is a modified skin gland that forms along the milk line, from the armpit to the groin, so extra breast tissue can show up anywhere on it. Mastitis is an infection during breastfeeding, treated with antibiotics. Duct ectasia can pull the nipple in. A seatbelt injury can cause fat necrosis. Of the benign lumps, cysts and fibrosis add almost no risk of cancer, growths without odd cells a little, and atypical ductal hyperplasia a moderate amount. Breast cancer Cancers start in the ducts or the lobules, and stay in place (in situ) or invade. Ductal carcinoma in situ needs surgery; lobular carcinoma in situ is now considered benign. Invasive ductal cancer forms glands; invasive lobular cancer grows in single-file lines. Paget disease is a red, scaly nipple from cancer cells, which means looking for a cancer in the breast (one is there in about 95 percent). The outlook depends on size, grade, lymph nodes and the receptors (estrogen, progesterone and HER2), which drugs can target. Men get the same diseases, but breast cancer is rare in men and usually found late (some carry BRCA2); gynecomastia, an enlarged breast from extra estrogen, is common in obese men and in weightlifters taking testosterone.
